opus-5.5.text:
I think physical-world understanding is not just one component of a world model. In some sense it *is* the core of it.

A lot of current AI progress has come from language. Large language models are incredibly powerful, but language is a very compressed, human-made abstraction of the world. It's a description of reality, not reality itself. When we talk about a world model, what we really want is a system that can perceive, represent, and predict how the world actually works: how objects move, how things interact, what happens if I push this cup off the table. Much of that knowledge is never written down, because for humans it's so obvious we don't bother to say it.

So I've always felt that vision, and perception more broadly, is the starting point. Babies don't learn about the world by reading text. They look, they touch, they move around, and they gradually build an intuitive sense of physics, space, and causality. That kind of grounded understanding is what I think is still largely missing from today's models.

There's also a distinction I care about. Generating something that *looks* realistic is not the same as understanding the physical world. A video model can produce beautiful pixels while violating basic physics, with objects appearing and disappearing or interactions that make no sense. To me, a real world model needs a good internal representation: an abstract, structured understanding that supports prediction, reasoning, and eventually planning and action. The pixels are just one way to read that understanding out.

That's why I think representation learning matters so much here. The question isn't only "can you render the next frame," but "do you have the right internal state of the world that lets you anticipate what comes next and act in it." If we get that right, it opens the door to embodied intelligence, robotics, and AI systems that can operate in the real world rather than only in the space of text.

So in my view, physical-world understanding is the foundation. Without it, what we have is a very knowledgeable system that doesn't truly live in our world. With it, we can start moving toward something closer to general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes physical-world understanding as foundational for embodied intelligence, robotics, and operating in the real world. It does not state that world models can benefit agents operating in digital environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think physical-world understanding is the whole point, honestly. For a long time the field treated "world model" as almost synonymous with video generation: if you can predict the next frame convincingly, you must understand the world. I've become fairly skeptical of that framing. Pixel prediction is a very expensive proxy for understanding, and a lot of what a generative model spends its capacity on is texture, lighting, and appearance details that have nothing to do with whether an object will fall, roll, or collide.

So when I say I want to build a world model, I mean a model whose internal representation actually captures the structure of the physical world: objects, space, geometry, how things move and persist, what happens when you act on them. That representation should be useful for reasoning and for acting, not just for rendering. This is partly why I've been so interested in representation learning again, in things like how a model builds a stable spatial map of a scene rather than just a sequence of plausible images.

The honest state of affairs is that current models, including the big multimodal ones, are still surprisingly weak at this. They can describe an image beautifully and then fail at a simple question about relative position or what's behind what. Language gives you a lot for free, but language is a compressed, lossy description of the physical world that humans produced after they already understood it. If you only learn from that, you inherit the description without the underlying grounding.

So I'd put it this way: physical understanding isn't a feature we add on top of a world model. It's the thing that makes it a world model rather than a very good video prior. And I think the path there runs through better visual and spatial representations, learned from interaction and prediction in latent space, rather than through ever-larger pixel generators.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model should support reasoning and acting, but it does not state that world models benefit agents operating in digital environments.

astra-6.text:
I think physical-world understanding is central to what we mean by a world model. It’s not enough for a model to recognize an object or describe a scene. It needs some understanding of how that scene can change: how objects interact, what persists when it goes out of view, and what might happen if you take an action.

For example, seeing a cup on a table and saying, “That’s a cup,” is recognition. Predicting what happens when you push it toward the edge requires something more. And if the model can use that prediction to decide how to move the cup safely, then that understanding becomes useful for acting in the world.

But I wouldn’t equate a world model with a perfect physics simulator. We don’t calculate every force when we pick up a cup. We have an approximate understanding that lets us anticipate consequences, and we adapt when our expectations are wrong. That’s the kind of capability I think matters: learning representations that support prediction and action, while accounting for uncertainty.

The challenge is how to learn that. Observing video can tell you a lot about how the world changes, but observing something happen and understanding what your own action will cause are different. So I see physical-world understanding as both a core objective and a way to test whether these models have learned something beyond surface-level patterns.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical-world understanding and acting in the physical world, but does not state that world models can benefit agents operating in digital environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think understanding the physical world is a fundamental part of a world model. It’s not enough to recognize what’s in an image or describe a video. A model should understand how things change, how objects interact, and what might happen if you take a particular action.

For example, if you push an object toward the edge of a table, can the model anticipate that it might fall? Can it distinguish between an object moving on its own and one being moved by something else? These sound like simple questions, but they involve understanding space, time, and causality.

I don’t think that necessarily means we have to build a robot first. Learning from visual observations could take us a long way. But interaction is important because it lets you test your predictions. Ultimately, I would judge a world model by whether its understanding helps it predict and act in new situations, rather than just produce a convincing description.
